TESTIMONY OF ALICIA REA, ESQ. LD 647 - Ought to Pass
An Act Regarding Telephone and Video Call Access in Detention and Correctional Facilities and Jails
Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety
March 24, 2025
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety, greetings. My name is Alicia Rea, and I am a policy fellow for the American Civil Liberties Union of Maine, a statewide organization committed to advancing and preserving civil liberties guaranteed by the Maine and U.S. Constitutions. On behalf of our members, I urge you to support LD 647.
LD 647 would allow inmates to connect with their loved ones more easily by establishing a standard of 90 minutes of free video and phone access per week. For people who are incarcerated, maintaining family and community bonds is crucial to mental health, physical health, community health and community safety. Maine should set this 90-minute threshold for all carceral facilities, allowing for those being held--often without being sentenced-- to communicate with both their loved ones.
Experts estimate that nationwide, the families of incarcerated people pay nearly $3 billion every single year on the hidden costs of incarceration.1 There are commissary costs, costs associated with visitation, legal costs, medical fees, and of course, costs for phone calls and text messages. According to the Prison Policy Institute, incarcerated people in Maine prisons can expect to earn between 50 cents and $3.50 per hour.2 At these wages, incarcerated individuals have to work between 3 and 18 hours to afford the 90-minutes of phone and video calls.
Even though families and communities are footing the bill, our entire state reaps the benefits of these social connections. Good communication
1 Beatrice Lockwood & Nicole Lewis, The Hidden Cost of Incarceration (Dec. 2019), available at https://www.themarshallproject.org/2019/12/17/the-hidden-cost-ofincarceration. 2 Prison Policy Institute, How much do incarcerated people earn in each state?, Apr. 10, 2017, available at https://www.prisonpolicy.org/blog/2017/04/10/wages/.

throughout incarceration makes people less likely to recidivate after reentering their communities.3 Maine should itself pay the costs of a standard 90-minute phone and video allowance as an investment in the health of its communities. We urge you to vote ought to pass.
3 Leah Wang, Research roundup: The positive impacts of family contact for incarcerated people and their families (Dec. 2021), available at https://www.prisonpolicy.org/blog/2021/12/21/family_contact/.

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and distinguished members of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee: My name is Jan Collins, I am Assistant Director of Maine Prisoner Advocacy Coalition (MPAC) an organization committed to ethical, positive, and humane changes in Maine's prison system. I am here in support of LD 647 An Act Regarding Telephone and Video Call Access in Detention and Correctional Facilities and Jails.
During the Covid pandemic we learned to appreciate contact with family. The connections we once took for granted became more precious. We learned that contact was essential to our mental health. NAMI Maine estimated anxiety and depression doubled in Maine during the pandemic as a result of the isolation experienced, in particular by children..1
The median monthly income for men and women prior to their incarceration is less than half of the average income of people who are not incarcerated.2 Desperate poverty is not unusual for a young family whose primary bread winner is incarcerated. It is particularly burdensome for those families to shoulder the cost of transportation or phone calls in order to maintain ties with an incarcerated or detained loved one.
The benefits of maintaining ties with family members are immense, but are particularly important for the mental health and well-being of children with parents who are incarcerated. More than 20,000 children have a parent incarcerated in one of Maine's prisons or jails. At 8%, Maine has the highest incarceration rate of parents in the New England states and 14th highest in the nation.3
"Children who have experienced parental incarceration are more at risk for

homelessness, depression and anxiety, economic instability, low educational attainment, and juvenile justice system involvement,"according to the Cutler Institute Justice Policy Program.
For children, bene ts of time spent with their parent may include decreased anxiety about abandonment or the parent's well-being, increased attachment, healing of grief and loss, decreased feelings of isolation, and improved behavior at home and school.4
Our communities are safer, and both parents and children have better outcomes, when healthy contact is maintained during incarceration.
I hope you will consider the impact of telephone and video charges on struggling families in Maine and vote unanimously to support this bill.
With appreciation, Jan M. Collins, MEd Assistant Director Maine Prisoner Advocacy Coalition

Sen. Anne Beebe-Center, Chair Rep. Tavis Hasenfus, Chair Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice & Public Safety 100 State House Station Augusta, ME 04333
Re: Comments of MCCA on LD 647, An Act Regarding Telephone and Video Call Access in Detention and Correctional Facilities and Jails
Dear Members of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee:
On behalf of the Maine County Commissioners Association, we appreciate the opportunity to provide testimony neither for nor against LD 647. While we acknowledge the intent to enhance communication access for individuals, we must express our reservations about this bill due to its potential financial implications for county jails and local taxpayers.
About MCCA. Briefly, the Maine County Commissioners Association was established in 1890 to assist Maine's county government in providing vital services to Maine citizens in a responsive, efficient, and credible manner. The Association is based in Augusta, represents all 16 of Maine's counties, and is governed by a board with representation from each participating county.
What does LD 647 do? LD 647 proposes to require county jails and correctional facilities to provide residents with at least 90 minutes of free telephone and video calls per week. The bill also prohibits jails from collecting revenue from these communication services, shifting the financial responsibility for maintaining these systems to the facilities, which are primarily funded by local taxpayers.
Current Funding Mechanism. Presently, county jails partner with service providers to offer telephone and/or video call services to residents. The fees collected from these services are not merely operational costs but serve as a crucial revenue stream. These funds are utilized to:
� Cover service expenses: Ensure the maintenance and availability of communication infrastructure within the facilities.
� Support indigent resident services: Provide essential services to residents who lack financial resources, including legal assistance, counseling, and rehabilitation programs.
Financial Impact of LD 647. By mandating free telephone and video calling services, the bill would eliminate a significant source of revenue that county jails currently depend upon to fund both communication services and programs for indigent residents. This bill will lead to an increased burden on local taxpayers. With approximately 80% of jail operational costs already shouldered by local taxpayers, the removal of this revenue stream would necessitate compensating for the shortfall through increased local funding. This shift would place an undue financial burden on our communities, many of which are already facing fiscal constraints

MCCA Letter re LD 647 March 18, 2025 Page 2
Unfunded mandate. Under Maine's constitution, when state laws or rules impose costs on a unit of government, the state is responsible for 90% of the costs unless otherwise approved by both houses of the Maine Legislature with a 2/3 vote. We believe the mandating of video calls and the removal of external funding sources would qualify as a local mandate requiring a mandate preamble.
Conclusion. While we support initiatives aimed at improving the welfare of jail residents, LD 647, in its current form, poses financial challenges for county jails and local taxpayers. We urge the committee to consider these implications carefully and explore alternative solutions that balance the need for enhanced communication access with the fiscal realities faced by our county correctional facilities. We appreciate the opportunity to provide testimony neither for nor against LD 647. If you have questions or need additional information, please do not hesitate to let us know.
Respectfully submitted,

Stephen Gorden Co-Chair, Legislative Policy Committee, MCCA

Jean-Marie Caterina Co-Chair, Legislative Policy Committee, MCCA

RE: LD 647 -- An Act Regarding Telephone and Video Call Access in Detention and Correctional Facilities and Jails
Dear Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and Members of the Judiciary Committee:
MACDL supports LD 647.
Attorney client communication is critical for effective representation. This bill would ensure that inmates are given access to free telephone and video calls with their attorneys.
Currently, not all jails offer free inmate telephone or free video calls with their attorneys.
As this committee knows, our criminal justice system is in crisis. Part of the crisis is a lack of attorneys for incarcerated individuals. Currently, attorneys spend too much time in their vehicles traveling to jails to visit clients because there is no effective way to communicate with them via telephone or video. Travel can include multi-hour trips to visit clients at a jail because the jail lacks a video visitation option. This bill should help free up time that attorneys spend traveling which will help resolve cases faster, more cost effectively, which in turn should allow attorneys to take on more cases over the course of a year.
Additionally, this bill would not only benefit attorneys but it would also benefit inmates and their families. This bill would ensure telephone and video visits between inmates and their families. "Family phone calls are shown to reduce the likelihood of recidivism"1. A 2014 study of incarcerated women found that those who had phone contact with a family member were less
1 See https://www.prisonpolicy.org/blog/2021/12/21/family_contact/

likely to be reincarcerated within five years after their release. In fact, phone contact has a stronger effect on recidivism compared to visitation, which the study also examined.2 This bill should be voted Ought to Pass. Thank you for the opportunity to address this Committee on this important issue. Sincerely, /s/ Jeremy Pratt, Esq. President, MACDL
2 See Barrick, Kelle, et. al., Reentering Women: The Impact of Social Ties on Long-Term Recidivism, The Prison Journal (2014).

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing
Committee of Criminal Justice and Public Safety. My name is Sheriff Joel Merry. I am the
Sheriff of Sagadahoc County and I am here on behalf of the Maine Sheriffs Association.
Your Maine Sheriffs have taken the unanimous position of OPPOSITION for LD 647 - An Act
Regarding Telephone and Video Call Access in Detention and Correctional Facilities and Jails.
This bill will have a significant impact on county taxpayers if passed. Due to a recent FCC
ruling, the fees charged to our residents have been greatly reduced. While the intent of this legislation appears to be beneficial to our incarcerated populations, it fails to recognize where telephone fees are used and the unintended and negative impact it would on these individuals.

Maine jails do not charge residents any fees for communicating with their legal counsel. Fees are incurred when personal calls take place only. All funds received from these calls go directly into
that jail's Inmate Benefit Fund or IBF. By eliminating these fees, you're eliminating the purchase of rec room equipment, televisions, games, and books. Items that aren't included in jail budgets.

It's important to understand what services are provided to anyone incarcerated at one of Maine's
fifteen jails. Every single inmate is equipped with a tablet for their own use. These tablets have
been programmed with books, movies, games, educational tools, and full access to all their legal
records. The only time a resident would not be furnished with their own tablet is when that
person has been violent or abusive towards people or belongings. If that person becomes
stabilized, they will receive a tablet.

As you've now heard several times this session, Maine jails are underfunded and understaffed. Video calls cost time and money. Staff must assist residents when making these calls. Mandating
that jails provide these se1"~/ices will further burden an already overstressed system. Keeping
track of minutes to roll over may seem uncomplicated, but staff will be tasked with recording
minutes.

If jails are forced to absorb the costs of the additional requirements in L.D. 647, there is no other
way to fund these expenditures other than burdening our local taxpayers. Maine Sheriffs urge you to vote Ought Not To Pass. I am happy to answer any questions you may have.

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and members of the Criminal
lustice and Public Safety Committee, my name is Lani Graham. I am from Freeport. l am here in support of this very modest bill to get us all on the same page with a
definition.
This definition simply establishes a common understanding of what solitary
confinement is for Maine people and Maine government. Whenever there is a medical problem for public health, the first step is establishing a clear definition of
the problem. For example, we all know now what must be present for a diagnosis of
Covid. lt is not sufficient to have a loss of smell, a runny nose, or a sore throat. You must have a positive test. Most people will agree that solitary confinement is a serious problem for the health of people who undergo it. This bill simply defines the condition, allowing us all to understand what is meant. It requires nothing of the Maine Department of Corrections nor of sheriffs, nor of county jails. This bill will not change any care, treatment or behavior in Maine jails or prisons.
This bill establishes in Maine law the United Nations definition of this practice,
which was passed and endorsed by that Assembly in 2015.
By passing this law, Maine comes into line with hundreds of other countries and jurisdictions that have recognized solitary confinement. The Maine Department of Corrections has been clear in its assertion that this practice is no longer used in
Maine and therefore we no longer need to wonder about the definition. However, as we certainly know, governing administrations at both the state and federal level can
change radically in just a year or two. Therefore, coming to agreement on what
exactly solitary confinement is could be valuable in the future as we continue to
struggle with criminal actions, substance use disorders and mental health problems.
I urge this committee to support this very modest bill unanimously ought to pass.
Thank you for your attention, I would be pleased to answer any questions you might
have.

I want to begin by recognizing the good intentions behind this proposal, which is an effort to reduce the financial obligations imposed on residents of the correctional system and ensure that they have the means necessary to contact
family and legal counsel. While the department respects where the sponsor is coming flom with that goal, we cannot

The Bill As Printed:
As printed, LD 647 would provide residents with a weekly 90 minute allowance of flee telephone and video calls, as well

From a financial perspective, the bill as printed would result in a substantial fiscal impact to our department. Currently,
DOC provides phone calls to residents under the statutory framework in 34-A MRS �3015, which provides that a resident
who has less than $10 in their facility account is eligible for a free telephone call allowance of 30 minutes per week, and that a resident who has less than $10 in their facility account is eligible for an additional flee telephone call allowance of 30 minutes per week for attomey-client calls. There are no flee video calls under the current statute. This process is also

impact on the department than the one outlined in the bill as printed, it still has the potential to substantially impact our current contract with our facility telecommunications provider by expanding the number of residents that would be
eligible for free phone calls. The department is still working to evaluate what that impact would ultimately be, but we are
seriously concerned that any change in the current eligibility criteria could result in a financial impact to our provider that
would ultimately trigger a contract renegotiation, leave DOC responsible for filling the gap, and potentially threaten the
sustainability of the services we were able to secure through the most recent rounds of negotiations. That reality poses a serious financial risk to the department in a time when funding is already extremely tight. While we would ultimately like to find some common ground with this proposal, any change to the current provisions would result in an added fiscal
impact outside what was provided for in the 26-27 Biennial Budget.
For the reasons stated above, the department respectfully presents this testimony in opposition to this proposal.

Testimony in support of LD 647 the Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety
March 24, 2025
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and distinguished members of the Committee:
My name is Sarah Johnson and I am a resident of Sanford. I am writing in support of LD 647, An Act Regarding Telephone and Video Call Access in Detention and Correctional Facilities and Jails
I would like to thank all the cosponsors of LD 647 for this supportive and restorative bill. There is an abundance of data describing the benefits of maintaining family ties and communication for an incarcerated individual and their family. Many are cited in this Prison Policy Initiative research report: The positive impacts of family contact for incarcerated people and their families. The article states "In particular, children -- the "hidden victims" of incarceration -- are at increased risk for mental health problems and substance use disorders, and face worse intellectual outcomes compared to children without an incarcerated family member. Supportive family relationships can promote psychological and physiological health for incarcerated people and their loved ones, at a time when everyone's health is otherwise deteriorating. Serving families at this most critical period simply makes communities healthier. " These benefits also translate into a safer environment in the detention and correctional facilities and jails, which benefits all staff and allows for more programming.
LD 647 makes our entire Maine community safer, and supports families in their most stressful times.
I hope you will support this bill.
Thank you for your time and consideration. Sarah Johnson Sanford, Maine.

24 March 2025
Dear Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and Distinguished Members of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee;
I am writing on behalf of the Restorative Justice Project Maine, in support of LD 647, a bill supporting video and telephone call allowance of up to 90 minutes for jail and prison residents. Private phone contracts are a multi-million dollar industry in Maine. Companies have paid county governments millions of dollars in revenue-sharing agreements for exclusive telephone contracts at our jails, which inmates and their families must pay into to communicate.1 This is money coming for the most part directly from innocent family members who have no choice but pay the fees to talk with their loved ones. It is wrong to use innocent family members as a funding source for county jails. Poor families, in particular the thousands of children in Maine with a parent in custody, are harmed by the inability to connect. To disrupt the intergenerational cycle of incarceration and poor outcomes for Maine's children, we must implement policies supporting families. This starts with communication. Providing a 90 minute allowance for telephone or video connection with families and loved ones for residents of Maine correctional facilities will be a major step forward.
Respectfully, Tim Hughes, M.D. Legislative Committee, Restorative Justice Project Maine
